title: White Oak vs Red Oak Flooring: Which Should You Install in Seattle?
meta: White oak vs red oak flooring in Seattle: white oak for light, modern floors, red oak for matching older homes. Wills Flooring installs both, $3.25 per sq ft.

blocks.lead: For a new floor in Seattle, white oak is the better choice for most homes: it takes a light or natural finish without turning pink, it is slightly harder, and it handles damp winters a little better. Red oak wins when you are matching an existing floor or planning a medium to dark stain.
blocks.detail: Wills Flooring installs both at the same labor rate, $3.25 per sq ft for engineered or solid, so the decision is about look, matching and material cost.

blocks.html: The question reaches our Lynnwood showroom in two forms. A Ballard or Wallingford owner has pulled up carpet, found red oak from 1940, and wants to know whether the new addition should match it or go white oak. Or a buyer in a Queen Anne or Magnolia remodel has seen the pale, matte European look everywhere and wants to know if red oak can get there. The honest answer depends on what finish you want, what is already in the house, and how much you care about material cost.

blocks.text: The four differences you can actually see and feel

items.title: Undertone: pink vs tan
items.text: Red oak has a pink to salmon cast that shows through clear and light finishes. White oak runs tan, olive or gray-brown. This is the single biggest reason people pick white oak for a natural or whitewashed floor. Under a dark stain the undertone mostly disappears and the two species look alike.

items.title: Grain: cathedral arches vs straighter lines
items.text: Red oak has a wider, more dramatic grain pattern with big cathedral arches on plain-sawn boards. White oak is tighter and more uniform, and rift or quarter-sawn white oak gives the straight, calm lines you see in modern and Scandinavian rooms. Red oak reads traditional; white oak reads current.

items.title: Hardness: close, with an edge to white oak
items.text: On the Janka scale red oak rates about 1,290 and white oak about 1,360. That gap is real but small. Both dent under a dropped cast-iron pan and both hold up well to dogs and kids. The finish you choose matters more for daily wear than the species does.

items.title: Water: white oak's closed cells
items.text: White oak's pores are plugged with tyloses, which is why it was used for boats and wine barrels. Red oak is open-celled; you can blow air through a short piece. In a kitchen or entry with wet boots, white oak forgives a spill left overnight a little better. Neither should live in a bathroom.

blocks.text: Can red oak be made to look like white oak?

blocks.html: Partly. A bleaching or whitewash step, or a stain with a green or gray base, will neutralize much of the pink. The grain pattern, though, stays red oak: wider arches and more variation. Up close a trained eye can tell, and in a bright south-facing Green Lake living room the difference shows more than it does in a hallway. If a true pale European floor is the goal, buy white oak. If you already own red oak, we cover the workarounds in this post on staining red oak to look like white oak.

blocks.title: One Seattle-specific warning:
blocks.text: Many 1900s to 1940s houses in Ballard and West Seattle have old-growth fir, not oak, in bedrooms and halls, with oak only in the public rooms. Let us confirm the species before you order material to match. Fir next to oak never blends.
What to ask before you order oak flooring

items.html: Ask for the cut, not just the species. Plain-sawn, rift and quarter-sawn white oak look like three different floors. Rift and quartered cost more and move less.
See the sample with the finish you plan to use. A raw white oak board and a finished one can look a full shade apart. We bring finished samples to the house for exactly this reason.
Check grade. Select grade is clean and uniform; character or rustic grade has knots and color swing. Both species come in both grades, and grade changes the look more than species does.
Plan acclimation. Solid oak of either species needs several days in the house before install, and Seattle winters push indoor humidity around. Engineered is more forgiving.
Get labor and material on separate lines. Our hardwood installation is $3.25 per sq ft either way; the material line is where white and red oak differ, and you should see that number by itself.

faq.q: Is white oak more expensive than red oak?
faq.a: Usually, yes. White oak material tends to cost more than red oak of the same grade and width, and rift or quarter-sawn white oak costs the most. Installation labor at Wills Flooring is the same $3.25 per sq ft for either species, so the difference shows up only on the material line of your quote.

faq.q: Which is harder, white oak or red oak?
faq.a: White oak is slightly harder, about 1,360 on the Janka scale versus about 1,290 for red oak. In a real Seattle house with kids and a dog the difference is hard to notice. The finish, the sheen level and the number of coats affect visible wear far more than the small hardness gap between the two.

faq.q: Can you mix white oak and red oak in the same house?
faq.a: You can, but not in the same continuous floor. Use a doorway, threshold or a change in board direction to separate them. Under a natural finish the pink of red oak and the tan of white oak will always read as two different floors, even at the same stain color.

faq.q: Does white oak turn yellow over time?
faq.a: All oak ambers a little as the finish ages and sunlight hits it, but white oak with a water-based finish stays close to its original tan for years. Oil-based finish ambers noticeably more. Red oak's pink also softens with time but never fully goes away under a clear coat.

faq.q: What oak is in my old Seattle house?
faq.a: Most 1900s to 1950s Seattle homes have red oak strip in the living and dining rooms, often with fir in bedrooms and halls. White oak was used less often in that era. We identify the species at the free estimate by looking at the end grain and pore structure, which takes about a minute.

faq.q: Is engineered white oak a good choice for a Seattle condo?
faq.a: Yes. Engineered white oak is the most common plank we install in Capitol Hill and downtown condos because it is stable, can be glued or floated over concrete, and comes in the wide, matte European styles buyers want. Most buildings also require a sound underlayment, which we include in the quote.
